title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis
participant_role: Management accountant for Crumb & Co. analyzing March results with a flexible budget and standard cost variances
judge_role: CEO of Crumb & Co., a wholesale bakery, who believes operations are fine because profit missed the budget by only $600

difficulty.rationale: Flexible budget with price and quantity variances.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a management accountant for CRUMB & CO., a wholesale bakery that supplies artisan bread to grocery stores and restaurants. The CEO (judge) wants you to explain what the March results really say about the bakery's performance.

CRUMB & CO. uses a standard costing system and prepares a budget at the start of each month. The March budget was based on selling 10,000 loaves. To win new grocery accounts, the sales team ran a promotion in March and sold 12,000 loaves at a lower average price. The standard costs and the actual March results are shown in Exhibits A and B.

At this morning's management meeting, the CEO (judge) said, "We sold 2,000 more loaves than planned and only missed our profit budget by $600, so operations are fine." The CEO (judge) has asked you to look more closely before the numbers are shared with the purchasing manager, the production supervisor and the sales manager.

You will meet with the CEO (judge) to:
• Explain why comparing actual results to the static budget is misleading
• Prepare a flexible budget for the actual level of sales
• Calculate the sales volume variance and the flexible budget variances
• Separate the flour and direct labor variances into price (rate) and quantity (efficiency) variances
• Draw conclusions from your analysis and recommend actions

You will present your information to the CEO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CEO's (judge's) office. The CEO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your information and have answered the CEO's (judge's) questions, the CEO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Should we just raise the standards to match what actually happened?
Which variances should I investigate first?

solution.overview: A strong answer shows that the static budget compares 10,000 planned loaves to 12,000 actual loaves, so it hides what happened. The presenter builds a flexible budget for 12,000 loaves (operating income $30,000), splits the $600 unfavorable total into a $6,000 favorable sales volume variance and a $6,600 unfavorable flexible budget variance, breaks flour and labor into price and quantity parts, and recommends who should investigate what.

answer: A static budget is set for one activity level (10,000 loaves) and never changes
Comparing it to 12,000 actual loaves mixes the effect of selling more with how well costs were controlled
Variable costs should rise with volume, so higher actual costs look bad even when they are expected, and real problems can hide behind extra sales
Only $600 short sounds fine, but at 12,000 loaves the bakery should have earned $30,000
Fixed overhead stays $6,000
Flexible budget operating income = $30,000

by_task.task: Sales volume and flexible budget variances
answer: Static budget $24,000 vs actual $23,400 = $600 unfavorable in total
Sales volume variance = flexible $30,000 - static $24,000 = $6,000 favorable (2,000 extra loaves x $3.00 contribution margin)
Flexible budget variance = actual $23,400 - flexible $30,000 = $6,600 unfavorable
Parts: selling price $3,000 U, flour $0, labor $2,800 U, variable overhead $300 U, fixed overhead $500 U; total $6,600 U
Flour price: ($0.50 - $0.48) x 25,000 lbs = $500 favorable
Flour quantity: (25,000 - 24,000 lbs) x $0.50 = $500 unfavorable; net $0
Labor rate: ($16 - $15) x 1,300 hours = $1,300 unfavorable
Labor efficiency: (1,300 - 1,200 hours) x $15 = $1,500 unfavorable; total labor $2,800 unfavorable
The extra volume hid $6,600 of unfavorable performance; operations are not fine
The promotion cost $3,000 in lower prices; sales manager should show that new accounts will stay at full price
Labor is the biggest cost problem: 100 extra hours at a higher rate; production supervisor should check overtime, new hires and scheduling
Flour was bought cheaper but 1,000 extra pounds were used; purchasing and production should check whether cheaper flour caused waste
Review overhead spending and keep standards realistic, then report variances monthly by responsibility

calculations.label: Performance report: static budget, flexible budget and actual
steps: Total variable costs: static $30,000 | flexible $36,000 | actual $39,100

calculations.label: Flour variances
steps: Standard quantity allowed = 12,000 x 2 lbs = 24,000 lbs

judge_question_answers.question: Should we just raise the standards to match what actually happened?
answer: No: standards should reflect efficient, attainable performance, not whatever happened in one month
Raising them to match actual results would hide waste and remove the signal that tells managers where to act
Review standards regularly and change them only for lasting causes (a new supplier price, a new recipe or equipment)

judge_question_answers.question: Which variances should I investigate first?
answer: Use management by exception: start with the largest variances that someone can control
Labor first: $1,500 efficiency and $1,300 rate unfavorable (production supervisor)
Next, the $3,000 price variance from the promotion (sales manager) and the 1,000 extra pounds of flour (purchasing and production)
Small items like the $300 variable overhead variance can be watched rather than investigated now

key_concepts.definition: A budget prepared for one planned level of activity that is not adjusted when actual volume changes.
A budget adjusted to the actual level of activity, so revenues and variable costs are compared at the same volume. Flexible budget cost = actual units x standard variable cost per unit + fixed costs.
The expected cost to make one unit under efficient conditions, set for each input as standard quantity x standard price.

The difference between flexible budget and static budget income, caused only by selling more or fewer units. Sales volume variance = (actual units - budgeted units) x standard contribution margin per unit.
The difference between actual results and the flexible budget; it measures how well prices and costs were managed at the actual volume.
The effect of selling at a different price than planned. Selling price variance = (actual price - budgeted price) x actual units sold.
Materials price variance = (standard price - actual price) x actual quantity purchased or used; favorable when materials cost less than standard.
Materials quantity variance = (actual quantity - standard quantity allowed) x standard price; unfavorable when more material is used than allowed.
Rate variance = (actual rate - standard rate) x actual hours. Efficiency variance = (actual hours - standard hours allowed) x standard rate.
A favorable (F) variance increases income compared with the budget; an unfavorable (U) variance decreases it.
Focusing attention on the largest and most controllable variances instead of investigating every small difference.

notes: ICDC level because students must build a full flexible budget, split the total variance into volume and flexible budget pieces, and break two inputs into price and quantity variances, then tie each to a responsible manager. Watch for students who compute quantity variances with the budgeted 10,000 loaves instead of the actual 12,000, reverse the favorable and unfavorable signs, or accept the CEO's $600 conclusion without challenging it.

items.label: Describe the nature of flexible budgets

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the static budget is set for 10,000 loaves and never changes, so comparing it to 12,000 actual loaves mixes the effect of selling more with cost control, then builds the flexible budget for 12,000 loaves (revenue $72,000, flour $12,000, labor $18,000, variable overhead $6,000, fixed overhead $6,000, operating income $30,000).
criteria.meets: Explains why the static budget comparison is misleading and prepares a flexible budget for 12,000 loaves showing operating income of $30,000.
criteria.below: Knows a flexible budget adjusts for volume but makes errors building it, such as flexing the $6,000 fixed overhead or using the $5.75 actual price.
criteria.little: Does not prepare a flexible budget, or accepts the static budget comparison as fair.

items.label: Discuss the role of standard costing in the preparation and analysis of budgets

criteria.exceeds: Uses the $3.00 standard variable cost per loaf to build the budget, finds standard quantities allowed of 24,000 lbs of flour and 1,200 labor hours for 12,000 loaves, and explains that standards should reflect efficient, attainable performance and be changed only for lasting causes.
criteria.meets: Uses the standard costs per loaf to build the flexible budget and calculates the standard flour and labor allowed for 12,000 loaves.
criteria.below: Uses the standards but bases standard quantities on the budgeted 10,000 loaves (20,000 lbs and 1,000 hours) instead of the actual 12,000.
criteria.little: Does not use the standard costs in the analysis.

items.label: Discuss the use of variance analysis in managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Splits flour into a $500 favorable price and $500 unfavorable quantity variance (net $0) and labor into a $1,300 unfavorable rate and $1,500 unfavorable efficiency variance ($2,800 total), and explains what each variance tells managers.
criteria.meets: Correctly calculates the flour price and quantity variances and the labor rate and efficiency variances with the right favorable or unfavorable labels.
criteria.below: Calculates some variances correctly but reverses the favorable and unfavorable signs or misses the labor rate or efficiency part.
criteria.little: Does not calculate price and quantity variances, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibits.

items.label: Discuss the nature of cost accounting budgets

criteria.exceeds: Splits the $600 unfavorable total into a $6,000 favorable sales volume variance (2,000 extra loaves times $3.00 contribution margin) and a $6,600 unfavorable flexible budget variance, and breaks the $6,600 into selling price $3,000 U, flour $0, labor $2,800 U, variable overhead $300 U and fixed overhead $500 U.
criteria.meets: Calculates the $6,000 favorable sales volume variance and the $6,600 unfavorable flexible budget variance and shows they net to the $600 unfavorable total.
criteria.below: Finds only one of the two variances, or gets the flexible budget variance wrong because of a flexible budget error.
criteria.little: Does not calculate the sales volume or flexible budget variances.

items.label: Draw conclusions based on information analysis

criteria.exceeds: Concludes that extra volume hid $6,600 of unfavorable performance and the bakery should have earned $30,000, then assigns actions: the sales manager shows new accounts will stay at full price, the production supervisor checks overtime, hiring and scheduling, and purchasing and production check whether cheaper flour caused waste, with monthly variance reports by responsibility.
criteria.meets: Concludes that operations are not fine, identifies labor as the biggest cost problem and the $3,000 promotion price effect, and recommends who should investigate each.
criteria.below: Challenges the CEO's view but gives vague conclusions or recommendations not tied to specific variances.
criteria.little: Accepts the CEO's conclusion that missing the budget by $600 means operations are fine, or draws no conclusion.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the variances to each other and to the managers who cause them, such as cheaper flour possibly causing 1,000 extra pounds of waste and the promotion trading $3,000 of price for extra volume.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly that the favorable volume variance hid unfavorable cost and price performance.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or looks at each variance in isolation.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the CEO a prioritized action plan using management by exception, starting with labor, then the promotion price and flour usage, and keeps standards realistic rather than raising them.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations for the largest variances and names who is responsible.
criteria.below: Gives general recommendations that are not prioritized or not clearly assigned.

criteria.exceeds: Explains static versus flexible budgets and favorable versus unfavorable variances in plain language the CEO can follow, and tactfully corrects the CEO's view with confident, professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the flexible budget, variances and recommendations clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a three column performance report (static $24,000, flexible $30,000, actual $23,400) or a simple visual that makes the hidden $6,600 obvious, and suggests a useful idea such as monthly variance reports by manager.
criteria.meets: Organizes the budgets and variances in a way that makes the comparison easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the numbers with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: do not raise standards to match one month because that hides waste, change them only for lasting causes like a new supplier price, recipe or equipment; and use management by exception, starting with labor ($1,500 efficiency and $1,300 rate), then the $3,000 price variance and the 1,000 extra pounds of flour, while just watching the $300 variable overhead variance.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that standards should stay attainable and that the labor variances should be investigated first.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without naming specific variances.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees to raise standards to match actual results.

key_points: The static budget (10,000 loaves) is misleading because actual sales were 12,000 loaves
Flexible budget for 12,000 loaves: revenue $72,000, variable costs $36,000, fixed overhead $6,000, operating income $30,000
Total variance $600 U = sales volume variance $6,000 F plus flexible budget variance $6,600 U
Flexible budget variance parts: selling price $3,000 U, flour $0, labor $2,800 U, variable overhead $300 U, fixed overhead $500 U
Flour: price $500 F and quantity $500 U (25,000 lbs used vs 24,000 allowed)
Labor: rate $1,300 U and efficiency $1,500 U (1,300 hours vs 1,200 allowed)
Operations are not fine: extra volume hid $6,600 of unfavorable performance; labor is the biggest cost problem
Do not raise standards to match actual results; investigate the largest controllable variances first
